title: Morality is motivated by getting revenge
subtitle: The hypocrisy at the heart of our justice system
author: Gregg D. Caruso
introduction: We have evolved to want revenge. The desire to see those that have hurt us be hurt in kind feels not just natural but morally just. But philosopher Gregg D. Caruso argues that this strike-back instinct is built on a belief we can no longer defend — that people are the ultimate authors of their own actions, free from the luck of their genes, upbringing, and circumstance. Abandon that belief, and the justice system we've built around it starts to look less like justice and more like organised cruelty.
body:
When someone wrongs us—cuts us off in traffic, betrays our trust, or harms someone we love—we feel a powerful urge to strike back. This impulse runs deep. It’s visceral, immediate, and feels entirely justified. We want the wrongdoer to suffer, to pay for what they’ve done. This strike-back emotion lies at the heart of our practices of moral blame and punishment. But what if this deeply ingrained response, however natural it feels, is based on a fundamental mistake about human agency and moral responsibility?

The strike-back emotion feels so natural, so justified, that questioning it seems absurd or even dangerous.

According to the work of free will skeptics like myself, the kind of free will required to justify our retributive practices—the backward-looking desire to make wrongdoers suffer because they deserve it—simply doesn’t exist. This doesn’t mean we cannot hold people responsible in other important senses, protect society, or maintain meaningful relationships. But it does mean we need to rethink some of our most cherished assumptions about blame, punishment, and what people truly deserve.

The stubborn system of desert

Our belief that individuals are morally responsible in the sense that would make them truly deserving of blame and punishment is remarkably stubborn. Despite philosophical arguments that challenge its foundations, despite scientific evidence about the causes of human behavior, and despite the manifest failures of our punitive criminal justice system, we cling tenaciously to the idea that wrongdoers deserve to suffer for their misdeeds. Why is this belief so persistent?

One major reason is the strike-back emotion itself. This powerful emotional response, which we share with other animals, creates a strong psychological need to believe in so-called basic desert moral responsibility: the idea that wrongdoers deserve to suffer for their misdeeds just because they have knowingly done wrong. When we’re wronged, we don’t just want the harmful behavior to stop or to prevent future harms. We want retribution. We want the wrongdoer to suffer because they deserve it. And to justify this desire, we need to believe that people are morally responsible in a “basic” sense—the sense that would justify blame and punishment on purely backward-looking grounds, without appealing to forward-looking considerations like deterrence, rehabilitation, or public safety.

This emotional foundation makes basic desert moral responsibility seem obvious and unchallengeable. The strike-back emotion feels so natural, so justified, that questioning it seems absurd or even dangerous. We worry that without it, wrongdoers would get away with their crimes, that society would descend into chaos, that our relationships would lose their meaning. These fears, however understandable, prevent us from examining whether our retributive practices are actually justified.

The pervasive notion of just deserts

The strike-back emotion doesn’t operate in isolation. It’s embedded within what I call the just deserts system—a complex network of practices, institutions, and beliefs that extends throughout society and assumes that individuals justly deserve to be praised and blamed, rewarded and punished, for their freely performed actions. This system includes our criminal justice practices, our everyday habits of praise and blame, our assumptions about success and failure, and our basic understanding of what it means to be a person.

Within this system, basic desert moral responsibility seems self-evident. We’re surrounded by constant reminders that people deserve what they get: criminals deserve punishment, the successful deserve their wealth, the poor deserve their poverty. These messages are reinforced by our legal institutions, our religious traditions, our political rhetoric, and our common sense. The system makes challenges to basic desert moral responsibility seem not just wrong but incoherent—like claiming that 2+2=5.

This pervasive system serves important psychological and social functions. It provides a sense of order and justice in an often chaotic and unfair world. It allows us to feel that our own successes are earned and deserved. It gives us a target for our anger when we’re wronged. And it provides a seemingly straightforward justification for punishment: wrongdoers deserve to suffer.

But these psychological comforts come at a steep price.

The belief in a just world

Underlying both the strike-back emotion and the notion of just deserts is what psychologists call the belief in a just world. This is the deep-seated conviction that people generally get what they deserve and deserve what they get. And research shows that the stronger the belief in free will, the stronger the belief in a just world. According to this belief, good things happen to good people and bad things happen to bad people. The world, in other words, is fundamentally fair and just.

Research has consistently shown that people have a strong need to believe in a just world. This belief helps us feel safe and in control—if the world is just, then by being good we can avoid bad outcomes. But maintaining this belief requires us to engage in some troubling mental gymnastics. When we encounter innocent victims—people who suffer through no fault of their own—our belief in a just world is threatened. The most common way we preserve this belief is by blaming the victim.

This phenomenon has been extensively documented in cases of rape, where victims are often blamed for dressing provocatively, drinking too much, or putting themselves in dangerous situations. The same pattern appears with poverty, illness, and other misfortunes. Rather than acknowledge that bad things happen to innocent people—which would threaten our belief in a just world—we find ways to make victims responsible for their own suffering.

If these beliefs are mistaken, then we’re inflicting enormous harm on millions of people based on a philosophical error.

The belief in a just world also correlates strongly with political conservatism and opposition to social welfare programs. If people deserve their circumstances, then the wealthy earned their success through hard work and good choices, while the poor brought poverty upon themselves through laziness and bad decisions. This belief conveniently justifies existing inequalities and absolves society of responsibility for addressing them.

Ironically, the costs of belief in a just world are paid in fundamental injustice. By assuming that people deserve their fates, we ignore the profound effects of luck, circumstance, and factors beyond individual control. We overlook systemic injustices, we blame victims, and we justify punitive excess in criminal justice.

Free will beliefs and punitiveness

The connection between belief in free will and punitive attitudes has been demonstrated by numerous empirical studies. Research shows that stronger belief in free will predicts greater support for retributive punishment, harsher recommended sentences, and more punitive attitudes generally. Importantly, these studies also show that free will beliefs specifically predict retributive attitudes—the desire to punish because wrongdoers deserve it—rather than consequentialist motivations like deterrence or public safety.

In one particularly revealing study, participants who read a passage undermining belief in free will recommended roughly half the prison sentence (about five years) compared to a control group (about ten years) for the same crime—even when told the offender had been successfully rehabilitated and posed no further threat. This suggests that much of our desire to punish is purely retributive, driven by the belief that wrongdoers deserve to suffer regardless of any beneficial consequences.

The problem isn’t just that luck plays a role in our lives—everyone acknowledges that. The problem is that luck goes all the way down.

These findings have profound implications. They suggest that our punitive criminal justice system—with its harsh sentences, degrading conditions, and emphasis on making offenders suffer—is largely driven by belief in free will and basic desert moral responsibility. If these beliefs are mistaken, then we’re inflicting enormous harm on millions of people based on a philosophical error.

Why free will skepticism?

So why should we be skeptical about free will and basic desert moral responsibility? The arguments are complex and detailed, but the core insight is straightforward: what we do, and the way we are, is ultimately the result of factors beyond our control. If our actions are causally determined by factors in our past—our genes, our upbringing, our circumstances—then they trace back to conditions we did not choose and cannot be held ultimately responsible for. But if our actions are instead the result of indeterministic events—random quantum fluctuations or chance occurrences—then they are no more within our control, since we cannot determine how these random events will unfold. Either way, whether determinism or indeterminism is true, the control required for basic desert moral responsibility appears to be absent.

Consider also the various types of luck that shape our lives. There’s constitutive luck—the luck of our genetic endowments, our temperament, our dispositions. There’s circumstantial luck—the luck of our upbringing, our environment, our opportunities. There’s resultant luck—the luck of how our actions turn out. And there’s present luck—the luck of what influences happen to be acting on us at any given moment.

These forms of luck are pervasive and unavoidable. We don’t choose our genes, our parents, our early childhood experiences, or the social and economic circumstances into which we’re born. Yet all these factors profoundly shape who we become and what we do. Even our efforts to overcome our circumstances or improve ourselves are influenced by factors ultimately beyond our control—our capacity for self-control, our motivation to change, the opportunities available to us.

The problem isn’t just that luck plays a role in our lives—everyone acknowledges that. The problem is that luck goes all the way down. We cannot undo the effects of luck with more luck. The very actions through which we might try to take responsibility for ourselves are themselves significantly subject to luck. Either they express our existing endowments (which result from constitutive luck) or they reflect our present circumstances (which result from circumstantial and present luck), or both.

This doesn’t mean we’re not agents who make choices and act for reasons. It doesn’t mean we can’t be held responsible in a non-desert-based sense or that we shouldn’t face consequences for our actions. But it does mean we’re not morally responsible in the basic desert sense—the sense that would make us truly deserving of blame and punishment, independent of any forward-looking benefits these might produce.

Living without retribution

Many people worry that abandoning belief in free will and basic desert moral responsibility would have catastrophic consequences. Without the threat of deserved punishment, wouldn’t people behave badly? Without the possibility of earned praise, wouldn’t achievement lose its meaning? Without moral responsibility, wouldn’t our relationships become cold and calculating?

These fears, I’ve argued, are largely unfounded. In my new book, How to Live Well Without Free Will,I argue that we can preserve most of what we care about—morality, love, creativity, safety, meaningful relationships, social justice, and forward-looking moral responsibility—without retributive blame and punishment.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Forgiving the unforgivable With Lucy Allais

Consider our criminal justice system. Rejecting retributivism doesn’t mean we must release dangerous criminals or abandon all forms of sanctions. What it means is that we must justify any harm we impose on non-retributive grounds, rather than on the backward-looking ground that offenders deserve to suffer. Derk Pereboom and I, for instance, have developed what we call the public health-quarantine model, as a non-retributive alternative to our current system, which grounds incapacitation and restriction in the right of self-defense and the prevention of future harm, rather than in backward-looking desert. The model maintains that just as we may quarantine carriers of dangerous infectious diseases without blaming them for their condition, so too may we incapacitate individuals who pose a serious threat to others. The justification is protective, not punitive. The public health-quarantine model therefore rejects desert-based punishment and instead justifies interventions solely on the right of self-defense and prevention of future harm.

With this approach comes important constraints that retributivism lacks. First, we can only impose the minimum harm necessary for adequate protection. We can’t make conditions harsher than needed just to increase suffering. Second, we must prioritize prevention and address the social determinants of crime—poverty, inequality, lack of opportunity, inadequate mental health care, etc. Third, we must focus on rehabilitation and reintegration rather than punishment. And fourth, we must treat offenders humanely, respecting their dignity even while restricting their liberty.

This approach would transform our criminal justice system. It would eliminate the death penalty, dramatically reduce incarceration, improve prison conditions, and shift resources toward prevention and rehabilitation. It would also reduce the racial and economic disparities that plague our current system, since these disparities are often justified by claims about who deserves punishment.

Rethinking the reactive attitudes

What about our personal relationships and emotional responses? Philosopher P.F. Strawson famously argued that moral responsibility is grounded in our reactive attitudes—emotions like resentment, indignation, and moral anger. He worried that abandoning these attitudes would leave us with a cold, objective stance incompatible with meaningful personal relationships.

But we don’t need to abandon all reactive attitudes, and we certainly don’t need to adopt a purely objective stance toward others. What we need to give up are specifically the retributive reactive attitudes—resentment and indignation—that presuppose basic desert and aim at making wrongdoers suffer because they deserve it.

There are alternative attitudes available that don’t presuppose basic desert but can serve similar functions. When someone wrongs us, instead of resentment we can feel moral disappointment, sadness, or hurt. We can also communicate our values, set boundaries, and seek to change behavior. Most importantly, we can engage in moral protest and exchange, holding wrongdoers answerable for their choices—all without the backward-looking desire to make the wrongdoer suffer for its own sake.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Justice in jeopardy With Isabel Hilton, Harriet Wistrich, Myriam François, David Livingstone Smith

These alternative attitudes can be just as effective for moral formation and relationship repair, and in some ways they’re superior. Retributive anger often escalates conflicts, damages relationships, and prevents reconciliation. It focuses on the past rather than the future, on suffering rather than growth. By contrast, forward-looking responses focus on understanding, prevention, and positive change.

This doesn’t mean we become passive or accepting of wrongdoing. We can still protest injustice, hold people answerable for their choices, and demand change. But we do so from a stance of moral concern rather than retributive anger—seeking to protect, prevent, and improve rather than to punish and make suffer.

Beyond the strike-back emotion

The strike-back emotion is powerful and deeply rooted. It’s reinforced by the pervasive notion of just deserts and sustained by our need to believe in a just world. But this emotional and psychological foundation doesn’t make retributive practices justified. In fact, I’ve argued that these practices cause enormous harm—in our criminal justice system, in our personal relationships, and in our social and political life.

By recognizing the strike-back emotion for what it is—an evolved response that may have served our ancestors but doesn’t justify our current practices—we can begin to move beyond it. We can develop alternative responses to wrongdoing that are more humane, more effective, and more just. We can build a criminal justice system focused on protection, prevention, and rehabilitation rather than retribution. We can cultivate personal relationships based on understanding and growth rather than blame and resentment.

This won’t be easy. The strike-back emotion and belief in basic desert moral responsibility are stubborn indeed. But the potential benefits—a more just society, a more humane criminal justice system, healthier relationships, and a clearer understanding of ourselves—make the effort worthwhile. We can live well, perhaps even better, without the illusion of basic desert moral responsibility and the retributive practices it supports.
